messages.subject: Data Access Layer Spec
parts:
I’ve attached the basic spec for the data access layer (which will replace var_context),
refactored transforms, and how they will be used in the generated model code.  It should
be self consistent.  Any thoughts?

// DATA ACCESS LAYERS

// base_dal
vector_t get_vector(const std::string& name, size_t N) {
  if (!contains_r(name)) {
    std::stringstream msg;
    msg << "Variable " << name
        << " not found in variable context" << std::endl;
    throw std::runtime_error(msg.str());
  }

  std::vector<size_t> dims = dims_r(name);
  if (dims.size() != 1) {
    std::stringstream msg;
    msg << "Requested the vector " << name
        << ", but " << name
        << " is not defined as a vector in variable context"
        << std::endl;
    throw std::runtime_error(msg.str());
  }

  if (dims[0] != N) {
    std::stringstream msg;
    msg << "Requested the vector " << name
        << " with size " << N << ", but " << name
        << " is defined with size " << dims[0] << " in variable context"
        << std::endl;
    throw std::runtime_error(msg.str());
  }

  std::vector<double> vals = vals_r(name);
  vector_t output(N);
  for (vector_t_idx n = 0; n < N; ++n)
    output(n) = vals[n];
  return output;
}

// constr_dal
template <typename T>
void get_constrained_vector(const string& name,
                            const stan::io::transform& transform,
                            vector_t param) {
  param.resize(transform.size());
  param = get_vector(name, transform.size());
  transform.validate(param);
}

// unconstr_dal
template <typename T>
void get_unconstrained_vector(const string& name,
                              const stan::io::transform& transform,
                              vector_t::InnerIterator& it) {
  vector_t constr_val = get_vector(name, transform.size());
  transform.unconstrain(constr_val, it);
}

// EXAMPLE TRANSFORM
template <typename T, typename T_LB>
class vector_lower_bound: public vector_transform<T> {
private:
  T_LB lower_bound_;

public:
  vector_lower_bound(T_LB lower_bound, size_t N):
    lower_bound_(lower_bound), vector_transform<T>(N) {}

  size_t unconstrained_dim() { return N_; }

  void validate(vector_t constr_val) {
    stan::math::check_greater_or_equal("stan::io::vector_lower_bound",
                                       "Lower bound constraint", constr_val,
                                       lower_bound_);
  }

  template <typename Jacobian>
  vector_t constrain(const vector_t& unconstr_val, lp_accumulator<T_LB>& acc) {
    vector_t constr_val;
    for (idx_t n = 0; n < N_; ++n) {
      if (Jacobian) {
        T_LB lp;
        output(n) = stan::prob::lb_constrain(unconstr_val[n], lower_bound_, lp);
        acc.push_back(lp);
      } else {
        output(n) = stan::prob::lb_constrain(unconstr_val[n], lower_bound);
      }
    }
  }

  vector_t constrain(const vector_t& unconstr_val,
                     std::vector<double> constr_val) {
    for (idx_t n = 0; n < N_; ++n)
      constr_val.push_back(stan::prob::lb_constrain(unconstr_val[n],
                                                    lower_bound_));
  }

  void unconstrain(const vector_t& constr_val, vector_t::InnerIterator& it) {
    for (idx_t n = 0; n < N_; ++n)
      *(it++) = stan::prob::lb_free(constr_val[n], lower_bound_);
  }
};

// MODEL USE CASES

// constructor
model_name {
  ...
  vector_lb_transform<input_type, lb_type>
    param_name1_transform__(lb_value);
  data_var_context.get_constrained_vector("param_name1",
                                          param_name1_transform,
                                          param_name1__);
  ...
}

// init
void init(vector_t& unconstr_state) {
  vector_t::InnerIterator it(unconstr_state);

  ...
  vector_lb_transform<input_type, lb_type>
    param_name1_transform__(lb_value);
  get_unconstrained_vector(“param_name1", param_name1_transform, it);
  ...
}

// what write_array was
void constr_state(vector_t unconstr_state,
                  std::vector<double>& constr_state) {
  ...
  vector_lb_transform<input_type, lb_type>
    param_name1_transform__(lb_value);
  param_name1_transform__.constrain(unconstr_state, constr_state);
  ...
}

// log_prob
template <typename T>
T log_prob(vector_t& unconstr_state) {
  lp_accumulator<T> lp_acc__;

  ...
  vector_lb_transform<input_type, lb_type>
    param_name1_transform__(lb_value);
  vector_t param_name1__ =
    param_name1_transform__.constrain<Jacobian>(unconstr_state, lp_acc__);
  ...
}

and you only get one init for lp, but not the benefit of turning it

It can be, but it just allocates a new variable on the stack each time.
Passing in the accumulator would be most efficient. So on the inside,
you get

sum(0 + j[1], 0 + j[2], ..., 0 + j[n])

whereas doing it on the outside you get

0 + j[1] + j[2] + ... + j[n]

and with an accumulator you get the ideal

sum(j[1], j[2], ..., j[n])

and if you pass in the global accumulator, it's a bit better still
because those j[1]...j[n] just go in the global accumulator's sum.

>> The type of vector_t and T_LB can be different? It might be a double
>> value for the accumulator. Can we then drop the Jacobian if it's
>> constant? Or do we need to worry about getting the full density either
>> way?

> thought about dropping any constants, but in any case I think that
> logic should be pushed back into the math transforms.
Agreed.

>> For vector_transform<T>, are there any virtual functions? I
>> didn't see the base class spec.
>
> Yeah, all of the functions mentioned above are defined as pure virtual
> in a base class (or they will be).

Right --- if T is the class template parameter type, I think that's
the only option. The alternative, that wouldn't use virtual functions, is
to add another template parameter for the transform. I'd go with that,
because it'll be most efficient and given that it's not some complex
template metaprogram, won't adversely affect compile time (no recursion,
just simple matching).

- Bob

>

There's a tension in C++ between using templates and
meta-defined "concepts" (meta in the sense that they aren't
defined in the object language) vs. proper object-oriented
programming. I agree that it's easier to understand as
a developer if there's a base class that gets passed rather
than a templated concept. The tension is because the templated
approach is faster. The in-between "solution" is the CRTP, like
Eigen uses for its matrix classes, though we've also seen what
a pain that is in practice.

> We could template out the
> DAL methods on the transform types but because they’re used only
> once I don’t think it’ll have any affect on performance.

Right. The run-time issue is with the unconstraining
transforms. Anyway, this is something that'll be easy to modify
later without affecting the interface.

- Bob

Here's an example of how inheritance works in C++ with
virtual functions. Note that you only need to define the
base class method as virtual and then all the inherited class methods
will also be virtual. The behavior doesn't change if B::foo is
declared as virtual.

#include <iostream>

struct A {
virtual int foo() const { return 0; }
};

struct B : public A {
int foo() const { return 1; }
};

void printer(const A& a) {
std::cout << "printer " << a.foo() << std::endl;
}

template <typename T>
void printer2(const T& x) {
std::cout << "templated printer " << x.foo() << std::endl;
}

int main() {
A* a1 = new B();
std::cout << "a1->foo() " << a1->foo() << std::endl;

A a2 = B();
std::cout << "a2.foo() " << a2.foo() << std::endl;

std::cout << "B().foo() " << B().foo() << std::endl;

B b = B();
printer(b);

printer2(b);
}


The output is:

~/temp2$ clang++ foo.cpp

~/temp2$ ./a.out
a1->foo() 1
a2.foo() 0
B().foo() 1
printer 1
templated printer 1


So I don't think we can avoid the virtual call overhead by templating.

Now Java has a clever way of declaring a class final, but
C++ allows linking in new instances, so it can't decide statically
if a class is final (i.e., doesn't allow extensions). So it can't
know how that printer2() function dispatches at compile time.

- Bob

There's a tension in C++ between using templates and
meta-defined "concepts" (meta in the sense that they aren't
defined in the object language) vs. proper object-oriented
programming.  I agree that it's easier to understand as
a developer if there's a base class that gets passed rather
than a templated concept.  The tension is because the templated
approach is faster.  The in-between "solution" is the CRTP, like
Eigen uses for its matrix classes, though we've also seen what
a pain that is in practice.

Right, but you don’t _have_ to use the base class with virtual
functions.  I just like having it there to define the concepts
concretely and in the code we can always use templates to
avoid the virtual overhead.

Here's an example of how inheritance works in C++ with
virtual functions.  Note that you only need to define the
base class method as virtual and then all the inherited class methods
will also be virtual.  The behavior doesn't change if B::foo is
declared as virtual.

#include <iostream>

struct A {
 virtual int foo() const { return 0; }
};

struct B : public A {
 int foo() const { return 1; }
};

void printer(const A& a) {
 std::cout << "printer " << a.foo() << std::endl;
}

template <typename T>
void printer2(const T& x) {
 std::cout << "templated printer " << x.foo() << std::endl;
}

int main() {
 A* a1 = new B();
 std::cout << "a1->foo() " << a1->foo() << std::endl;

 A a2 = B();
 std::cout << "a2.foo() " << a2.foo() << std::endl;

 std::cout << "B().foo() " << B().foo() << std::endl;

 B b = B();
 printer(b);

 printer2(b);
}

~/temp2$ clang++ foo.cpp

~/temp2$ ./a.out
a1->foo() 1
a2.foo() 0
B().foo() 1
printer 1
templated printer 1


So I don't think we can avoid the virtual call overhead by templating.

Now Java has a clever way of declaring a class final, but
C++ allows linking in new instances, so it can't decide statically
if a class is final (i.e., doesn't allow extensions).  So it can't
